work: The Greater Record Of Mourning Rites
heading: Liji 19 · Sang Da Ji 喪大記 · The Greater Record Of Mourning Rites · Sang Da Ji II.4 … Sang Da Ji II.14

items.text: At the great dressing of his father's body, lean on it and leap as an expression of grief.
items.quote: The son then (seemed to) lean on it, and leaped while his wife did the same, with her face to the east.

items.text: At the great dressing of her father-in-law's body, lean on it and leap with her face to the east.
items.quote: The son then (seemed to) lean on it, and leaped while his wife did the same, with her face to the east.

work: The Greater Record Of Mourning Rites
heading: Liji 19 · Sang Da Ji 喪大記 · The Greater Record Of Mourning Rites · Sang Da Ji II.26 … Sang Da Ji II.37

items.text: Escort the ruler outside the gate and bow to the ground before him.
items.quote: the chief mourner escorted him outside the gate, and bowed to him, with his forehead to the ground.

items.text: Put on the clothes worn at the coffining when the ruler comes to condole.
items.quote: the (son) put on again the clothes he had worn at the coffining.

items.text: Go down the west steps and bow your head to the ground before the ruler's wife.
items.quote: The wife presiding went down by the steps on the west, and bowed with her head to the ground below (the hall).

items.text: Escort the ruler's wife to the inner door and bow to the ground when she retires.
items.quote: the wife presiding went with her to the inside of the door of the apartment, and bowed to her with her head to the ground.

items.text: Escort the ruler's wife to the outside of the great gate, but do not bow.
items.quote: The chief mourner escorted her to the outside of the great gate, but did not bow.

items.text: Stand facing north when a Great officer visits the mourning rites.
items.quote: The chief mourner (stood on the south of his place), with his face to the north, though the general rule for chief mourners was to face the south.

items.text: Put down the offerings by the coffin after the ruler leaves if they were not prepared beforehand.
items.quote: when the ruler withdrew, the rule was that they should then be put down.
items.conflict: Offerings to the dead conflict with the second commandment and the sufficiency of Christ's work.

items.text: Provide a coffin of the proper thickness and lining for his rank.
items.quote: The coffin of a common officer was six inches thick.

items.text: Place scorched grain and dried fish by the coffin as offerings.
items.quote: Of scorched grain there were put by the coffin of a ruler eight baskets, containing four different kinds.
items.conflict: Offerings to the dead conflict with the second commandment and the sufficiency of Christ's work.

work: The Greater Record Of Mourning Rites
heading: Liji 19 · Sang Da Ji 喪大記 · The Greater Record Of Mourning Rites · Sang Da Ji I.25 … Sang Da Ji II.3

items.text: During the mourning for his father, a ruler, eat nothing for three days; then take only a handful of rice morning and evening, without observing set meal times.
items.quote: his (eldest) son... ate nothing for three days, but confined themselves to gruel. (Afterwards)... a handful of rice, and another in the evening

items.text: During mourning for her father-in-law, the ruler, eat only coarse rice and drink water, without fixed meal times.
items.quote: The wife (of the new ruler)... had coarse rice and drank water, having no regard in their eating to stated times.

items.text: During mourning for a grandfather, a Great officer, be confined to gruel.
items.quote: the presiding mourner, the steward, and grandsons, all were confined to gruel.

items.text: After the burial of his father, eat only coarse rice and drink water; do not eat vegetables or fruits.
items.quote: After the burial, the presiding mourner had (only) coarse rice and water to drink;--he did not eat vegetables or fruits.

items.text: After the burial of her father-in-law, eat only coarse rice and drink water; do not eat vegetables or fruits.
items.quote: His wife observed the same rule.

items.text: When his father is alive, mourn his mother with the same dietary restrictions as for a full year, even though the mourning is shorter.
items.quote: When the father was alive, in the mourning of nine months, the rules were the same as in that for a year, on account of the mother or of the wife.

items.text: During mourning, even when allowed to eat flesh and drink liquor, do not share the enjoyment of them with others.
items.quote: Though they ate flesh and drank liquor, they could not take the enjoyment of these things in company with others.

items.text: Between the coffining and burial, if you eat flesh or drink liquor, do not enjoy them in company with others.
items.quote: Between the coffining and burial, when eating flesh and drinking liquor, they did not take the enjoyment of these things in company with others.

work: The Greater Record Of Mourning Rites
heading: Liji 19 · Sang Da Ji 喪大記 · The Greater Record Of Mourning Rites · Sang Da Ji I.13 … Sang Da Ji I.24

items.text: In mourning for a parent, perform the prescribed gestures and offerings at the proper times, with due differences for father and mother.
items.quote: When the mourning was for his mother, he went to his place, and tied up his hair, after which he put down the offerings by the body.
items.conflict: Worship of the dead is forbidden; honor parents but do not offer sacrifices (Exod 20:3-5; Deut 18:10-12).

items.text: If the proper presiding person is absent, a son or daughter must preside over the funeral reception and bow to guests in the appointed place.
items.quote: When there was no female to preside, a son did so, and bowed to the female visitors... If there were no son to preside, a daughter did so, and bowed to the male visitors

items.text: If the successor is within the state, wait for him before the encoffining and burial; the funeral rites must not proceed without someone to preside.
items.quote: The funeral rites might proceed without the presence of the successor of the deceased, but not without one to preside over them.

items.text: Use the mourning staff only as the rite permits: carry it in your hand inside the chamber and use it outside, and put it away when a message comes from the king.
items.quote: His (eldest) son and Great officers used it outside the door of the apartment; inside the door they carried it in their hands. When a message came from the king, (the son presiding) put away his staff

items.text: In mourning, younger sons carry the staff but do not use it when going to their places, deferring to the eldest son who alone uses it.
items.quote: All the sons assumed the staff, but only the eldest son used it when they were going to their places.

items.text: Immediately upon death, prepare the corpse: place it on the couch, cover it, remove the death garments, prop the mouth open, and support the feet.
items.quote: the corpse was transferred to the couch, and covered with a large sheet... A servant plugged the mouth open with the spoon of horn; and to keep the feet from contracting, an easy stool was employed.

items.text: Wash the corpse thoroughly with water and linen napkins, dry it, pare the nails, and dispose of the water as prescribed.
items.quote: they went in to wash the corpse... In washing they used napkins of fine linen, and in drying the body the ordinary bathing clothes. Another servant then pared the nails of the feet, after which they threw away the rest of the water into the pit.

items.text: When consulting the tortoise-shell about the corpse, put away the mourning staff.
items.quote: When attending to any consultation of the tortoise-shell about the corpse, he put away his staff.
items.conflict: Divination is forbidden; trust God's providence (Deut 18:10-12).

items.text: Ensure that someone presides over the funeral rites, even if the successor is absent.
items.quote: but not without one to preside over them

items.text: If the son is too young to walk, an adult must carry him in his mourning clothes and bow on his behalf.
items.quote: If the son were a child, then he was carried in his sackcloth in the arms, and his bearer bowed for him.

work: The Greater Record Of Mourning Rites
heading: Liji 19 · Sang Da Ji 喪大記 · The Greater Record Of Mourning Rites · Sang Da Ji II.15 … Sang Da Ji II.25

items.text: Mourn your parent by dwelling in the slanting shed, unplastered, sleeping on straw with a clod of earth for a pillow, and speaking of nothing but the rites.
items.citation: Liji, Sang Da Ji II.15 … Sang Da Ji II.25
items.quote: occupied the slanting shed, unplastered; slept on straw, with a clod of earth for his pillow. He spoke of nothing but what related to the rites.

items.text: If you are not the eldest son by the proper wife, before the burial make a hut for yourself in an out-of-the-way place.
items.citation: Liji, Sang Da Ji II.15 … Sang Da Ji II.25
items.quote: All the other sons, but the eldest by the proper wife, even before the burial had huts made for themselves in out-of-the-way places.

items.text: After the mourning is changed at the end of a year, occupy the unplastered apartment and not one along with others, and after two years cease wailing outside, and after twenty-seven months cease inside and allow music to be heard.
items.citation: Liji, Sang Da Ji II.15 … Sang Da Ji II.25
items.quote: occupied the unplastered apartment, and did not occupy one along with others.

items.text: After mourning your father or mother, if the mourning is for one year, return to your husband after the change at the year's end; if nine months, return after the burial.
items.citation: Liji, Sang Da Ji II.15 … Sang Da Ji II.25
items.quote: when she had changed the mourning at the end of a year, she returned to her husband; when the mourning was that of nine months, she returned after the burial.

items.text: After one year's mourning for your parents, return to your own residence, but on the first day of the month, at full moon, and on the death-day, come back to wail in the house of the Head of the family.
items.citation: Liji, Sang Da Ji II.15 … Sang Da Ji II.25
items.quote: returned to their own residences after the change of the mourning at the end of the year; but on the first day of the month and at full moon, and on the return of the death-day, they came back and wailed in the house of him who was now the Head of their family.

items.text: Bend over the body of your parent, bringing your breast near to theirs.
items.citation: Liji, Sang Da Ji II.15 … Sang Da Ji II.25
items.quote: A son bent over his parents, bringing his breast near to theirs.

items.text: Do not take up quarters at your son's house during mourning.
items.citation: Liji, Sang Da Ji II.15 … Sang Da Ji II.25
items.quote: A father did not take up his quarters (during the mourning) at a son's.

items.text: Nor an elder brother at a younger's.
items.citation: Liji, Sang Da Ji II.15 … Sang Da Ji II.25
items.quote: nor an elder brother at a younger's.

items.text: After the one-year mourning for your mother, if your father is alive, abstain from the nuptial chamber for three months.
items.citation: Liji, Sang Da Ji II.15 … Sang Da Ji II.25
items.quote: when his father was alive, and he had been wearing the hemmed sackcloth of a year for his mother... for three months he did not seek the intercourse of the inner chamber.

items.text: After the one-year mourning for your wife, if your father is alive, abstain from the nuptial chamber for three months.
items.citation: Liji, Sang Da Ji II.15 … Sang Da Ji II.25
items.quote: when his father was alive, and he had been wearing the hemmed sackcloth of a year for his wife... for three months he did not seek the intercourse of the inner chamber.

work: The Greater Record Of Mourning Rites
heading: Liji 19 · Sang Da Ji 喪大記 · The Greater Record Of Mourning Rites · Sang Da Ji I.1 … Sang Da Ji I.12

items.text: As chief mourner, sob; do not wail like brothers and cousins.
items.quote: the principal mourners sobbed

items.text: Wail for the deceased.
items.quote: brothers and cousins (of the deceased) wailed

items.text: Wail for the deceased.
items.quote: brothers and cousins (of the deceased) wailed

items.text: As a female relative, wail and leap for the deceased.
items.quote: his female relatives wailed and leaped

items.text: Preside on the eastern side of the corpse.
items.quote: his son sat (or knelt) on the east

items.text: Preside on the western side of the corpse.
items.quote: His wife knelt on the west

items.text: Go out to receive visitors and messages during mourning.
items.quote: the principal mourner came out to receive the visit

items.text: Go out to receive female visitors and messages.
items.quote: The wife of a ruler went out (of her apartment) on a visit

items.text: When wailing by the corpse, hold up the shroud with both hands.
items.quote: the presiding mourner did so, holding up the shroud with his two hands

items.text: After the dressing, lament and change into mourning attire by unbaring your breast, removing the tufts of juvenility, and binding your hair with sackcloth.
items.quote: The mourner unbared his breast, took off the tufts of juvenility, and bound up his hair with sackcloth.

items.text: After the dressing, knot up your hair and put on the sackcloth girdle.
items.quote: The wife knotted up her hair, and put on her sackcloth girdle in her room.

items.text: When the curtain is removed, go down the steps and bow to the visitors.
items.quote: (the eldest son) going down the step's and bowing (to the visitors).
